title: URL-path API versioning over header-based versioning
notes: Clean decision session choosing URL-path versioning (/v1/) over header-based versioning for a new public API, with explicit reasoning.

turns.text: As we open up the public API, how should we version it — URL path like /v1/orders, or a custom header like Api-Version: 1?

I'd recommend URL-path versioning, /v1/orders — it's immediately visible in logs, browser address bars, and API docs without needing to inspect headers, which makes debugging and onboarding external developers noticeably easier.
Isn't header-based considered more 'RESTfully pure' by some people?

Some argue that, but the practical tradeoffs favor URL-path here: it's cacheable per-version by CDNs and reverse proxies without special Vary-header configuration, and it's much harder for a client to accidentally omit (a missing header silently falling back to a default version has caused real incidents at other companies when clients forgot to set it).
Good point about caching. What happens when we eventually need v2?

v1 keeps running unchanged at /v1/, v2 launches at /v2/, and we deprecate v1 on its own timeline once clients have migrated — no shared-route version-negotiation logic to maintain, each version is just its own route tree.
Confirmed: public API uses URL-path versioning starting at /v1/, with future versions living at their own /vN/ path root.

gold_atoms.text: Use URL-path versioning (/v1/orders) for the public API, not header-based versioning (e.g. Api-Version header).

URL-path versioning is cacheable per-version by CDNs and reverse proxies without special Vary-header configuration, and is harder for a client to accidentally omit than a header, which has caused real incidents elsewhere when clients forgot to set the version header.

Future API versions will each live at their own /vN/ path root (e.g. /v2/), with the prior version continuing to run unchanged until deprecated on its own timeline — no shared version-negotiation logic.
